clue.text: Did some work at last, back in Greek island

indicators.note: back tells us to read the cobbling verb from its last letter to its first

parts.note: a cobbler's last is the shoe form, so working at it means fitting new soles: soled

explanation.surface: Someone finally got some work done after returning to a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at last' looks like 'finally', but a last is the cobbler's foot-shaped block: working at it SOLED a shoe, and 'back' turns SOLED round.
explanation.definitionFit: Delos is a small island in the Cyclades, birthplace of Apollo in myth.

clue.text: Some of the fowl put up by beater

explanation.surface: A beater on a shoot sends up some of the game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A cooked bird's lower leg is called by this name, and so is the stick a percussionist hits with.

clue.text: Finish off insect in this place

indicators.note: to finish off something is to remove its final part, so the last letter of the insect goes

parts.note: a locust is a swarming insect

explanation.surface: An instruction to kill a bug right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish off' sounds like killing the insect, but it means cutting the last letter T from LOCUST.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin and in technical English a locus is a position or site.

clue.text: Get excited and form partnership headed by son

indicators.note: headed by puts the abbreviation for son at the front of the phrasal verb

parts.note: to team up is to join forces with someone

explanation.surface: Someone gets worked up when going into business with their son.
explanation.definitionFit: To get steamed up is an idiom for becoming agitated or angry.

clue.text: No reply comes to this player's address

definitions.text: No reply comes to this player's address

parts.words: No reply comes to this player's address
parts.note: an actor speaking alone on stage addresses nobody, so nobody answers: the speech is a theatrical monologue

explanation.surface: An actor speaks to someone and gets no answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'address' reads like a postal address but means a speech delivered by the actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech a character makes alone on stage, as Hamlet's 'To be or not to be', expects no response.

clue.text: Contemptuous form of address upset boatman

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means the boatman's name is turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: Harris is one of the boating companions in Jerome K Jerome's Three Men in a Boat

explanation.surface: A rude way of speaking to someone annoyed a boatman.
explanation.walkthrough: The boatman is Harris from Jerome K Jerome's comic novel Three Men in a Boat, about a Thames boating trip; reading HARRIS upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic way of addressing a man or boy one looks down on, often heard in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Stores records

explanation.surface: A two-word statement that shops keep archives.
explanation.definitionFit: One puts aside wine to mature by this phrasal verb, and one also uses it for setting rules or tracks down in writing or recording.

clue.text: Oriental national loses head and gets confused

indicators.note: gets confused tells us the remaining letters are mixed up into a new order
loses head means the first letter of the word national is removed

explanation.surface: A citizen of an Eastern country loses his temper and becomes muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses head' sounds like panicking, but it strips the N from NATIONAL; 'gets confused' rearranges ATIONAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Laos in South-East Asia, here called by the old term for an Asian.

clue.text: Bellringer for a particular Sunday

explanation.surface: A man who rings church bells on one special Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo's hunchback rang the bells of Notre-Dame, and the first Sunday after Easter takes its Latin name from the Introit opening words 'Quasi modo'.

clue.text: They come to ends in play, so they go upwards

definitions.text: They come to ends in play, so they go upwards

parts.words: They come to ends in play, so they go upwards
parts.note: toys on strings that drop to the end of the cord and then climb back up again

explanation.surface: Things that reach their limits while being played with and so rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends in play' sounds like a drama finishing, but it is the bottom of the string when the toy is in use.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinning toy runs down its string to the end and winds back up into the hand.

clue.text: A relative of Lear, connected in obscure way

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote the nonsense poem 'Incidents in the Life of My Uncle Arly'
the uncle's name in Lear's poem is Arly

explanation.surface: Someone related to King Lear is linked to him in some vague fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear here is Edward Lear the nonsense poet, not the king; his Uncle Arly, written as one 'connected' word, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Done without clarity, so in a vague or murky manner.

clue.text: Skill in communicating nothing suggestive

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
racy means risqué or suggestive

explanation.surface: A talent for conversation that never says anything rude.
explanation.definitionFit: The term, coined on the model of literacy, means fluency in speaking and listening.

clue.text: After opening word, lines laid out in Ruskin's work

indicators.note: After puts the rearranged letters following the magic word

parts.note: 'Open sesame' is the magic phrase from Ali Baba that opens the cave

indicators.note: laid out suggests the letters are spread around and set in a new order

explanation.surface: A note on a passage of Ruskin's book, after its opening word, about how its lines are arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening word' is the password of the Ali Baba story; 'out' rearranges LINES LAID into AND LILIES.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ruskin published these lectures on reading and on women's education in 1865.

clue.text: Not able to swallow slice of cake, or ingest

indicators.note: to swallow means one word takes another piece inside it

parts.note: inept means incompetent, not able

indicators.note: a slice of the word cake is just its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone unable to eat a piece of cake or take in food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slice of cake' looks like food, but it is only the C of 'cake', put inside INEPT.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology the verb means to take in or absorb food, a rare word for eating.

clue.text: Insect, bird and fish

parts.note: a cock is a male bird
a roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A list of three creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A scuttling household pest of the order Blattodea.

clue.text: Penchant for the ultimate performance?

parts.note: read penchant as a pen's chant: a female bird's song, and that song is said to be sung only at the very end of its life

explanation.surface: A liking for giving the very best show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penchant' means a fondness, but split as PEN-CHANT it is the song of a pen, a female swan; 'ultimate' means last, not best.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend has a dying swan sing once, so the phrase means someone's final appearance or work.

clue.text: Like an excellent opportunity to watch a duck

parts.note: a golden opportunity is a superb chance
to eye is to watch

explanation.surface: A great chance to observe a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A diving bird of northern waters named for its yellow iris.

clue.text: Effect of celebrating in German city round midnight

indicators.note: round means the city's name goes around the letter from the middle of the night

parts.note: Hanover is a city in Lower Saxony
the middle letter of night is G

explanation.surface: Partying in a German city until midnight has its consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'midnight' sounds like a time but is the middle letter of NIGHT, G, which HANOVER goes 'round'.
explanation.definitionFit: The headache and nausea after a night of heavy drinking are the price of a party.

clue.text: Worthless piece making music critic recoil initially

indicators.note: initially means the word for recoil comes first in the answer

parts.note: a gun's kick is its recoil
George Bernard Shaw wrote music criticism under the name Corno di Bassetto

explanation.surface: A critic's review of a worthless piece of music makes him wince at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' looks like a first-letter signal, but it only says the recoil comes first; the critic is George Bernard Shaw, a playwright who began as a music reviewer.
explanation.definitionFit: A trifle or trinket, from French quelque chose, something of no value.

clue.text: This market town might be found in trip to North

parts.note: to trip is to skip lightly

explanation.surface: A guess that a market town would be found on a journey northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: SKIPTON is a market town in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Skipton in North Yorkshire is known as the gateway to the Dales and has held markets for centuries.

clue.text: Chips served at one — also fish, possibly

explanation.surface: Chips are dished up there, and fish perhaps too, as in a canteen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' is Mr Chipping, the teacher in 'Goodbye, Mr Chips', who served at Brookfield; fish swim in a group with this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Chips taught at an academy, and a large shoal of fish is called by the same word.

clue.text: Disturbing calm with antics? Not half

definitions.text: Disturbing calm with antics? Not half

indicators.note: disturbing means the letters are shaken up into a new order
only half of the word antics is used, its first three letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks if fooling about would break the peace, and the reply is an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbing' rearranges CALM with ANT, the first half of ANTICS; the whole clue describes the noisy result, and 'Not half!' is also British slang for 'very much so'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means loud and insistent, which is what breaking the peace with clowning is.

clue.text: Gun easy to hear as a rule

indicators.note: easy to hear says the answer sounds the same as a word for a rule

parts.note: a canon is a rule or law, as in church canon

explanation.surface: A gun is generally simple to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'easy to hear' reads like loudness but signals a word that sounds the same: CANON, a rule, said aloud gives the gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A large piece of artillery firing heavy shot.

clue.text: Hogarth's work not offered to. Daisy

explanation.surface: A painting by Hogarth that was never offered to a girl called Daisy.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'Daisy Bell' says 'It won't be a stylish marriage, I can't afford a carriage', so a fashionable wedding is the one Daisy is not offered.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogarth's 1740s series of paintings satirises a fashionable wedding, the stylish match Daisy's suitor says he cannot give her.

clue.text: Girl married unfortunate sheep-herd

parts.note: Abel, a keeper of sheep in Genesis, was murdered by his brother Cain

explanation.surface: A young woman wed a luckless shepherd.
explanation.walkthrough: The shepherd is the Biblical Abel, 'unfortunate' because Cain killed him.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, a short form of Amabel.

clue.text: Bulb lit up repeatedly around one

indicators.note: around means the doubled word goes either side of the numeral
repeatedly tells us to write the word for lit up twice

parts.note: a light that is lit up is on
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A light bulb flickers on and off around one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' looks like a light bulb, matching 'lit up', but it is the vegetable: ON ON goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: The edible layered bulb of the allium plant used in cooking.

clue.text: Explosion in first World War magazine

explanation.surface: A bomb went off in a wartime magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'magazine' suggests an ammunition store, but it is Wyndham Lewis's Vorticist periodical of 1914-15.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden burst of air and noise from a detonation, and the title of Wyndham Lewis's short-lived avant-garde journal.

clue.text: Create destruction, as museum lies ruined

parts.note: the V and A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London

indicators.note: ruined means the letters of lies are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks a gallery whose collection lies in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: The V and A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum; 'ruined' rearranges LIES into LISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To deface or smash property on purpose, named after the Vandals who sacked Rome.

clue.text: Long Rhine trip for Wagner's hero

indicators.note: trip suggests stumbling, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Wagnerian hero takes a lengthy journey along the Rhine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' reads as a journey but rearranges LONG RHINE.
explanation.definitionFit: The swan knight of Wagner's 1850 opera, son of Parsifal.

clue.text: Heavyweight gets verdict, in the end, on points

indicators.note: in the end picks only the final letter of the word verdict

parts.note: N and E are two compass points, north and east

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer gets the decision on points at the end of the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing picture is false: T ends 'verdict', and 'points' are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: A metric weight of a thousand kilograms.
